Activation function.d: A small rule inside each artificial neuron that decides how strongly it passes its signal on. It lets networks learn curved, complicated patterns instead of only straight lines.

Agent.d: An AI system that works towards a goal by repeatedly deciding what to do, using tools (reading files, searching, running commands) and checking the results, rather than giving one answer and stopping.

AGI.d: Artificial general intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could learn and perform almost any intellectual task a person can. No agreed definition or test exists, and no current system is generally accepted as AGI.

Algorithm.d: A precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, like a recipe a computer can follow.

AI winter.d: A period when disappointment with AI led to big cuts in funding and interest. There were two major ones, in the mid-1970s and the late 1980s to early 1990s.

API.d: Application programming interface: a defined way for one program to ask another program to do something. The Claude API lets your software send messages to Claude and receive replies.

Artifact.d: In the Claude apps, a piece of content Claude creates in a panel beside the chat, such as a document, web page, diagram or small app, which you can view, use and share.

Artificial intelligence.d: The field of building computer systems that do things we'd normally say need intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images, solving problems or making decisions.

Attention.d: The mechanism inside a Transformer that lets each word (token) look at every other word in the text and decide which ones matter most for understanding it.

Backpropagation.d: The method neural networks use to learn: after a wrong answer, it works backwards through the network to calculate how much each connection contributed to the error, so each can be adjusted slightly.

Benchmark.d: A standard test used to compare AI models, such as a fixed set of exam questions or coding problems. Useful, but easy to over-trust.

Binary.d: A way of writing numbers using only two digits, 0 and 1. Computers store and process everything (text, pictures, sound) as binary.

Bit.d: The smallest unit of information: a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.

Chatbot.d: A program you talk to in ordinary language. Early chatbots followed scripted rules; modern ones are powered by large language models.

CLAUDE.md.d: A plain text file of instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session, used to tell it how a project works and what rules to follow.

Claude Code.d: Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It runs in your terminal, code editor, desktop app or browser, and can read files, edit them and run commands to complete tasks.

CLI.d: Command-line interface: a way of using a program by typing commands rather than clicking buttons. Claude Code is a CLI program.

Compute.d: Computing power: how many calculations can be done, usually provided by specialised chips such as GPUs. Modern AI needs enormous amounts of it.

Constitutional AI.d: Anthropic's method of training an AI to follow a written set of principles (a 'constitution'), partly by having the AI critique and improve its own answers against those principles.

Context window.d: The total amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider at one time: your messages, its replies, files and instructions. Anything outside it is invisible to the model.

Dataset.d: A collection of examples used to train or test an AI model, such as millions of labelled photos or a large body of text.

Deep learning.d: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. The 'deep' refers to the number of layers. It powers modern speech recognition, image recognition and language models.

Embedding.d: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text (or an image), arranged so that similar meanings get similar numbers.

Expert system.d: A 1970s–80s style of AI built from hundreds or thousands of hand-written if-then rules captured from human experts.

Fine-tuning.d: Further training an already-trained model on a smaller, specialised set of examples to change or improve its behaviour for particular tasks.

Generative AI.d: AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or code, rather than only classifying or predicting from existing data.

GPU.d: Graphics processing unit: a chip originally designed for video-game graphics that turned out to be ideal for the huge numbers of simple calculations AI needs.

Gradient descent.d: The step-by-step method used to improve a model during training: repeatedly nudging its settings in whichever direction reduces its error, like walking downhill in fog by feeling the slope.

Hallucination.d: When an AI produces information that sounds confident and plausible but is wrong or made up.

Hook.d: In Claude Code, a command or check that runs automatically at a set moment, such as before a tool runs or after a file is edited.

Inference.d: Using a trained model to produce an answer. Training is learning; inference is answering.

Knowledge cutoff.d: The date after which a model has no information from its training data. It may not know about events after that date unless given a search tool or the information directly.

Large language model.d: An AI model trained on a very large amount of text to predict and generate language. Claude, GPT and Gemini are large language models (LLMs).

Layer.d: A stage in a neural network. Information passes through layer after layer, each transforming it a little more.

Machine learning.d: A way of building AI where the computer learns patterns from examples instead of following rules a person wrote by hand.

MCP.d: Model Context Protocol: an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in 2024, for connecting AI applications to outside tools and data such as calendars, databases or a web browser.

Model.d: The trained AI system itself: a very large set of learned numbers plus the program that uses them to turn input into output.

Moore's law.d: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling at a regular pace (later settled at about every two years), making computers steadily more powerful and cheaper.

Multimodal.d: Able to work with more than one kind of input or output, such as text and images together.

Natural language processing.d: The branch of AI concerned with understanding and producing human language. Often shortened to NLP.

Neural network.d: A computer system loosely inspired by the brain, made of many simple connected units ('neurons') whose connection strengths are adjusted during training.

Neuron.d: In AI, a tiny calculation that takes in numbers, weighs each one, adds them up and passes on a result. Millions or billions of them make up a neural network.

Open-weight model.d: A model whose trained weights are published so anyone can download and run it, such as Meta's Llama. Different from 'open source', which would also include training code and data.

Parameter.d: One of the numbers inside a model that is adjusted during training. Large models have billions of parameters. Also called a weight.

Perceptron.d: An early artificial neuron that could learn simple yes/no decisions from examples, built by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958.

Pre-training.d: The first and largest stage of training a language model, in which it learns from a huge amount of general text by repeatedly predicting the next token.

Prompt.d: The input you give an AI model: your question, instructions and any material you include.

Prompt engineering.d: The skill of writing instructions and context so that an AI produces the result you want.

Prompt injection.d: An attack where text hidden inside content the AI reads (a web page, email or document) tries to give the AI new instructions.

RAG.d: Retrieval-augmented generation: looking up relevant documents first and giving them to the model along with the question, so its answer is based on those sources.

Reasoning model.d: A model trained to work through a problem step by step before giving its final answer, spending extra time 'thinking' on hard questions.

Reinforcement learning.d: A way of learning by trial and error: the system tries actions and is rewarded or penalised, gradually learning what works.

RLHF.d: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: improving a model by having people rate its answers and training it to produce the kinds of answers people prefer.

Self-attention.d: Attention where the words in a piece of text look at each other (rather than at a separate text). It's the core operation of the Transformer.

Skill.d: In Claude, a packaged set of instructions (and optionally files and scripts) for a particular kind of task, which Claude loads when relevant or when you call it by name.

Subagent.d: In Claude Code, a helper agent with its own separate context that the main agent can hand a task to, receiving back only the result.

Supervised learning.d: Learning from labelled examples, where each example comes with the correct answer, such as photos labelled 'cat' or 'dog'.

Symbolic AI.d: The early approach to AI based on writing explicit rules and logic for the computer to follow, using symbols that stand for things in the world.

System prompt.d: Instructions given to a model before the conversation starts, setting its role, rules and style. Usually hidden from the person chatting.

Temperature.d: How much randomness a model uses when picking each next word: lower is more predictable, higher is more varied. Many AI APIs let developers set it, but Anthropic's API removed the setting in API version 2026-10-21 (Chapter 83).

Terminal.d: A window where you type text commands for the computer to run, instead of clicking icons.

Token.d: A small chunk of text, often a whole short word or part of a longer one, that a language model reads and writes. In English a token is on average roughly three-quarters of a word.

Tokenizer.d: The part of a language model system that splits text into tokens and turns each one into a number the model can process.

Tool use.d: A model's ability to ask the application around it to perform an action (search the web, read a file, run code) and use the result.

Training.d: The process of adjusting a model's parameters using example data until it performs a task well.

Transformer.d: The neural network design, introduced by Google researchers in 2017, that underlies modern language models. Its key idea is attention.

Transistor.d: A tiny electronic switch, invented in 1947, that is the basic building block of all modern computer chips.

Turing Test.d: Alan Turing's 1950 proposal for judging machine intelligence: if a judge chatting by text can't reliably tell the machine from a person, the machine passes.

Unsupervised learning.d: Learning patterns from data that has no labels, such as grouping similar customers together without being told what the groups are.

Vector.d: An ordered list of numbers. In AI, vectors are used to represent things such as words, images or meanings.

Weight.d: A number that sets how strongly one neuron's output influences the next. Training means finding good weights.
